extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in comedy, aspiring stand-up comedians, and people looking for life/craft lessons from Steve Martin's memoir
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted lessons and practical criteria for producing and evaluating stand-up comedy performance and a comedian's career, drawn from a Steve Martin memoir/book-summary blog post. Focuses on craft, process, mindset, audience management, and career decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do What You Love
rubrics_metrics.description: Steve Martin is telling you to do what you love—to do what you were born to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martin's ascent into comedy felt 'fluid and smooth because that was who he was.' Choose work that aligns with who you are; authenticity makes the path easier and more sustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue the Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the craft, the process, and the learning and growth not the money or accolades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The easiest way to reach your standard of success is not to pursue it but to let it emerge as a side-effect of your effort, learning, and skill development." Prioritize practice, refinement, and learning over chasing fame or immediate rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: You're the Only One in Your Way
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s nothing holding you back but yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept limitations (e.g., not naturally talented at some skills) and be creative in finding solutions; you don't have to be 'great' to love what you do—use constraints to invent workarounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: It Takes Time / 18 Years to 'Overnight Success'
rubrics_metrics.description: Overnight success takes decades of building yourself and your skills, one brick at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martin describes 'The First 10 Years' of empty clubs, hostile audiences, and relentless practice. Be willing to be terrible for years, experiment in varied venues, and treat repeated failure as the training ground for breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walk Away / Know When to Leave
rubrics_metrics.description: When you are done, truly done, it’s okay to walk away and let go. Learn the difference between quitting and walking away from something for the right reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martin walked away from stand-up at his peak. Recognize when an art is complete for you or when continuing would harm the work; leaving can be an artistic decision, not a failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never Let Them Know You Are Bombing
rubrics_metrics.description: I gave myself a rule. Never let them know I was bombing: 'This is funny, you just haven’t gotten it yet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control audience perception: if a joke fails, incorporate the confusion or silence into the act rather than exposing defeat. Turning bombing into part of the performance can become a deliberate technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of Naïveté
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes, not knowing what the heck you’re doing is actually beneficial because you don’t know the rules—you have no boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naïveté allows you to try things that experts would consider impossible. Use ignorance to bypass conventional constraints and experiment freely (example: Sara Blakely calling Neiman Marcus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence Trumps Natural Talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination trumps natural talent every time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martin was brutally honest about his limitations and compensated with long-term persistence. Willingness to fail repeatedly in public served as a substitute for innate ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Delusional (Maintain Conviction)
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to believe you’re doing something important if you’re making balloon animals for drunk people at 2 AM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A degree of delusion or grand conviction helps sustain effort through absurd or low-status work. Many successful people use this psychological stance to persist despite obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt Material for Venue Size (The Arena Problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The absurdist touches that killed in a 200-seat club became meaningless in a 20,000-seat venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques that work in intimate settings (subtle absurdism, small gestures) may not scale to arenas. Anticipate how audience distance and scale change comedic effects and adjust material or delivery accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn Timing, Audience Management, and Holding Attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The magic shop taught him timing, audience management, and the crucial skill of holding attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical early work (e.g., performing at theme parks) builds foundational performance skills: precise timing, how to manage different audiences, and methods to keep attention—these are core competencies for stand-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by Practice and Experimentation (No Mentor Needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: There were no mentors to tell me what to do; there were no guidebooks for doing stand-up. Everything was learned in practice... the lonely road... was the place to dig up my boldest, or dumbest, ideas and put them onstage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize hands-on experimentation across varied, low-stakes venues. Use absence of formal guidance as freedom to iterate; tolerate 'dumb' ideas as material for discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect on the Struggle (Actionable Takeaway)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on the Struggle: 'I just believe that the interesting time in a career is pre-success, what shaped things, how did you get to this point?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action: journal on how you got to where you are, list successes and failures, map future goals and challenges. Use reflection to understand formative experiences and guide future practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get Closure (Actionable Takeaway)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If you have anything to work out with your parents, do it now. One day it will be too late.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address personal matters that affect your creative life; unresolved issues can shape career choices and emotional availability for art—practical step: seek closure where possible.
